articles.title: Iran gives US two-day diplomacy ultimatum
articles.summary: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Sunday warned the U.S. to either accept Tehran’s latest offer to end the more than eight-month war or face military escalation as President Trump mulls further strikes after the midterms. “American voters have made their choice. Time for the White House to make its own,” Araghchi wrote in a…
articles.body:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Sunday warned the U.S. to either accept Tehran’s latest offer to end the more than eight-month war or face military escalation as President Trump mulls further strikes after the midterms.

“American voters have made their choice. Time for the White House to make its own,” Araghchi wrote in a post on the social platform X , days after Tuesday’s midterm elections, where Republicans suffered historic losses over widespread voter anger at the Iran war.

“Our 2-day proposal stands: meet the requirement, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results. Or choose war, and see our alert and battle-harded Warriors rain down hell,” he continued.

Araghchi suggested that U.S. voters turned on Republicans in the midterms over opposition to the Iran war — a factor which has been largely agreed upon, including by President Trump.

Vice President Vance, who has been viewed as a possible contender for the Republican nominee in the 2028 presidential race, blamed the Iran war for the Democrats’ historic victories in the midterms that caused the GOP to lose control of both the House and the Senate.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance said in a lengthy social media post following the election results.

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” he continued. “But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

The warning from Tehran comes as mediators push Washington and Tehran to reach an agreement to end the conflict, with Qatar leading diplomatic efforts backed by Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey.

Iran has offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for global oil shipments whose closure has caused gas prices to surge, if the U.S. agreed to several conditions, including lifting sanctions and releasing billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets.

Trump, meanwhile, has left open the possibility of renewed military action against Iran, though he said Monday that he was in no hurry to make a decision.

articles.title: Egypt train crash: How a collision with a stationary train left 7 dead, 125 injured
articles.summary: At least seven people, including a train conductor, were killed and 125 injured after two passenger trains collided in Egypt’s Giza province, south of
articles.body: At least seven people, including a train conductor, were killed and 125 injured after two passenger trains collided in Egypt’s Giza province, south of Cairo, on Sunday. The crash took place in al-Ayyat district, around 52 km from the Egyptian capital.The Health Ministry confirmed the casualties, adding that more than 70 injured passengers had been discharged after receiving medical treatment.How did the collision happen?According to the Transportation Ministry, a train travelling towards the southwestern province of Fayoum crashed into the rear of another train heading to Aswan in southern Egypt.The chief prosecutor’s office said investigators reached the site late night. An initial inspection indicated that the Giza-Fayyoum train struck the last carriage of the Cairo-Aswan train, which was stationary on the same track and travelling in the same direction, officials said.The authorities have not yet announced the cause of the collision.Survivors describe rescue effortsResidents living near the crash site rushed to help passengers, pull survivors from the wreckage and call ambulances, Ayman Gamal, a resident of Kafr Girza in al-Ayyat, told the Associated Press.Gamal said he saw around 80 injured people being transported to nearby hospitals. Some passengers were trapped inside a carriage of the stationary train and were dead when they were pulled out, he said.Survivors taken to al-Wasta Central Hospital in Beni Suef province described scenes of confusion, with passengers struggling to breathe because of dust raised by the collision. Villagers eventually helped them escape, they said.Farha Gamal, who was travelling on the Fayoum-bound train, said she saw passengers who appeared to be dead, while others struggled to find their way out.“There were other cars that were completely mangled,” she told the AP.Investigation and emergency responsePresident Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation into the crash.The Egyptian Railway Authority said emergency teams and cranes had been sent to the site to remove the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible.Egypt’s history of train accidentsThe collision has renewed attention on safety concerns surrounding Egypt’s railway network, which has a history of mismanagement and poor equipment maintenance. The government has announced modernisation initiatives in recent years, but train crashes and derailments continue to occur.In September, a driver and his assistant were injured when two freight trains collided in the same district.Egypt’s deadliest railway disaster occurred in 2002, when a fire broke out on an overnight train travelling from Cairo to southern Egypt, killing more than 300 people.The latest investigation is expected to establish the circumstances behind Sunday’s collision and determine whether safety lapses or operational failures contributed to the deaths and injuries. Authorities have also said they are working to clear the tracks and resume normal rail operations.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Pasadena couple built a glass-walled house for about $45,000 in 1965 and kept it in the family for nearly six decades; after a careful restoration, the 2,156-square-foot property is now listed for $3.25 million
articles.summary: Some houses are built to make a statement, others are built to blend in with their surroundings.
articles.body: Some houses are built to make a statement, others are built to blend in with their surroundings. One midcentury modern residence in Pasadena, California pulls off both. The glass-and-wood home was built in 1965 for about $45,000 by a couple who kept it in the family for almost six decades. The celebrated architect Craig Ellwood designed the property, which has undergone a painstaking restoration and is now back on the real estate market and priced at $3.25 million. And it's not just the architecture that appeals. It's also the story of a home living through generations, without losing its original character. Scroll down to read the details.A modernist design with a different takeAccording to Archinect, the Kubly House, designed by Craig Ellwood Associates, was created for Don and Sally Kubly. The 1965-built property sits on a roughly 0.6-acre site at 215 La Vereda Road in Pasadena. The elevated single storey timber structure with large glass walls gives the impression of a pavilion suspended within the surrounding landscape.Unlike many of Ellwood’s celebrated buildings, which were heavily dependent on steel and glass, the house is built with a post-and-beam wooden framework. According to reports, the couple’s budget for construction was under $45,000, which factored into their decision. The result was a more economical interpretation of modernist architecture that did not sacrifice the clean lines and openness that were synonymous with the architect’s work.The house is inspired by the glass house tradition of architects like Philip Johnson and Mies van der Rohe, but with a warmer material palette, says Robb Report. Floor-to-ceiling windows allow natural light to penetrate the interiors, with views of surrounding eucalyptus and oak trees. The property boasts an outdoor swimming pool and spa in the lush greenery.A link to Pasadena’s architectural heritageThere is more to the house than just what it looks like. Don Kubly, closely associated with ArtCenter College of Design, served as the school’s second president. He and his wife were both graduates of the institution and their relationship with Ellwood continued after the completion of the residence.After that, Kubly hired Ellwood’s firm to design the Pasadena campus of ArtCenter College of Design, Homes says. The family’s relationship with one of Southern California’s leading modernist architects would only intensify as that architect’s firm went on to design the institution’s celebrated Hillside Campus, which was completed in 1976, states the Archinect report.Ellwood was among the leading architects in the region’s movement. He designed three houses for the Case Study House program, a project that explored new and affordable solutions for postwar housing. According to available records, the only home Greene designed in Pasadena seems to be the Kubly House, notes Robb Report.A restoration faithful to the original visionThe property remained with the Kubly family until 2022, when it changed hands for the first time in roughly 57 years. The new owners then undertook a restoration that aimed to retain the architect’s original vision, rather than turn the house into a contemporary luxury home.The renovation was carried out in collaboration with Carl Bronson of Bronstruction and adheres to the principle of conserving the existing architecture, reports Archinect. The work included upgrading building systems, repairing surfaces and a remodel of the primary suite that removed an interior partition to create a larger space. The distinctive timber framing, large glazing, and original material palette have been preserved.The restoration also included practical necessities like a new roof, updated electrical systems and air conditioning. Homes said it took about five months to get the property ready for its most recent listing, including fixing a deck that had been damaged by a fallen tree. The replacement timber was custom milled and sourced from a lumber yard in northern Washington, adds Robb Report.The interiors were also carefully laid out with original and period-inspired furniture selected with reference to Ellwood’s interior plans. Landscaping also received similar attention, with overgrown vegetation and non-native trees cleared to reveal the relationship between the house and its natural surroundings, claims the online report as well.A $3.25m listingAccording to Homes, the three-bedroom, two-bathroom home, now around 2,156 square feet, is on the market for $3.25 million with Chris Suarez and Kimberly Benz of Suarez + Benz at Compass.And Pasadena has also identified the property as eligible for individual listing in the National Register of Historic Places, adding another layer to its architectural appeal, Robb Report said.The Kubly House, owned by the same family for nearly six decades, is about to embark on another chapter with its restoration carefully preserving its defining features. Only the third owner in the property’s history, the next owner will inherit a distinctive piece of Pasadena’s midcentury architectural legacy.Image Courtesy: Cameron CarothersReady to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Billionaire couple Lynda and Stewart Resnick pledged $50 million to UC Davis in 2022; their 34,000-square-foot agricultural research centre opened in May 2026
articles.summary: A philanthropic pledge announced in 2022 has now taken physical shape at the University of California, Davis, where a new agricultural research centre
articles.body: A philanthropic pledge announced in 2022 has now taken physical shape at the University of California, Davis, where a new agricultural research centre opened its doors in May 2026. The facility, named after California philanthropists Lynda and Stewart Resnick, follows their $50 million donation to the university, the largest contribution it had received from individual donors at the time. Designed to bring agricultural science, technology and education under one roof, the building will support work on crop resilience, resource efficiency and food production. Four years after the original announcement, the project has moved from a proposed research hub to a completed campus facility, with laboratories and learning spaces intended for students and researchers.How the Resnicks' $50 million donation funded a new agricultural research centreThis began in October 2022, when UC Davis announced that Lynda and Stewart Resnick had pledged $50 million towards agricultural research and innovation. The contribution was a landmark donation for the university, which planned to use the funding to establish a dedicated centre addressing some of the challenges facing modern agriculture.The couple's contribution was divided into two parts. Around $40 million was allocated towards developing the research facility, while the remaining $10 million was earmarked for research grants through the Resnick Agricultural Innovation Research Fund.The announcement came at a time when agricultural institutions were increasingly examining how changing weather patterns, pressure on water supplies and growing food requirements could affect farming. UC Davis intended the centre to bring together specialists from different fields to investigate practical approaches to these problems.The building was originally planned as a 40,000-square-foot facility. Its completed design resulted in a 34,000-square-foot centre on the university's Davis campus in California.Who are Lynda and Stewart Resnick, the billionaires behind The Wonderful CompanyLynda and Stewart Resnick are among California's best-known business figures, with much of their wealth connected to agriculture, food and consumer products. They are co-owners of The Wonderful Company, whose brands include Wonderful Pistachios, POM Wonderful and Halos mandarins. The company's portfolio also includes FIJI Water.Their business interests have given the couple a longstanding connection to California's agricultural industry. Their donation to UC Davis was part of a wider commitment to research, education and environmental sustainability, rather than a contribution limited to the construction of a university building.The couple had also made a substantial commitment to another California institution. In 2019, they announced a $750 million donation to the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), supporting research into climate change and sustainability. The UC Davis contribution continued that philanthropic involvement in scientific research.What the new agricultural research centre is designed to doThe Resnick Center for Agricultural Innovation has been developed as a multidisciplinary space where agricultural researchers, engineers and students can work on problems affecting food production and the environment.Its research programme covers five broad areas: improving crop resilience in a changing climate, using water and energy more efficiently, finding new applications for agricultural byproducts, developing advanced technologies and increasing access to nutritious food.These subjects connect several areas of agricultural research. Scientists working on crop varieties, for instance, need to understand how plants respond to changing environmental conditions. Engineers and technology specialists can contribute tools that help farmers monitor fields, manage irrigation and collect information about crop performance.The centre also provides facilities for exploring how materials left over from agricultural production might be put to other uses. Pistachio shells, almond byproducts and pomegranate residues were among the materials identified when the original donation was announced.The $10 million research fund established through the Resnicks' gift was intended to support projects investigating the value of these agricultural materials. Rather than treating crop leftovers simply as waste, the research programme aims to identify useful properties and possible applications.Inside the 34,000-square-foot facilityThe completed centre is a two-storey building covering approximately 34,000 square feet. It stands on the western side of the UC Davis campus, close to the university's existing plant sciences facilities and agricultural research areas.Its interior includes laboratories, classrooms, research spaces and facilities for students seeking academic and career guidance. The building also provides space for testing and developing agricultural technologies, including robotics, sensors and other equipment used in modern farming.Artificial intelligence and data science are among the technologies expected to support work taking place inside the facility. Researchers can investigate how these tools might improve agricultural monitoring, make resource management more precise and help develop farming methods that respond to changing conditions.The building's design also reflects its environmental focus. UC Davis describes the centre as LEED-certified and all-electric, with solar power supporting its energy requirements. Its exterior features curved glass etched with white patterns resembling trees, giving the building a visual connection to the agricultural research carried out inside.The university's intention is to create a space where research can move beyond laboratory investigations and be tested in practical settings, including agricultural fields and growing environments.The centre officially opened in May 2026After the initial announcement in 2022 and a construction groundbreaking in May 2024, the Resnick Center for Agricultural Innovation reached its opening milestone on May 19, 2026.UC Davis marked the occasion with a ribbon-cutting ceremony attended by university leaders, students, faculty members, donors and industry representatives. Lynda and Stewart Resnick were also present for the event, which formally introduced the completed facility to the university community.The opening marked the completion of a project that had taken several years to move from its original funding announcement through design and construction. The university described the centre as a new base for collaboration between agricultural scientists, engineers and specialists working across related disciplines.You use AI every day. articles.title: Video shows small plane clip pickup truck during emergency landing on busy Florida road
articles.summary: Video captures a small plane making an emergency landing on a North Fort Myers road, clipping a pickup truck as it touches down on the asphalt.
articles.body: A small plane turned a Florida road into an emergency runway Saturday, crashing into the back of a moving pickup truck in a dramatic close call captured on video. Two pilots were aboard the aircraft when a mechanical issue forced them to attempt an emergency landing near Bayshore Road and Interstate 75 in North Fort Myers around noon, according to the Lee County Sheriff’s Office. The plane departed Sebring, Florida, around 11 a.m. Saturday and made the emergency landing about 50 minutes later, at 11:50 a.m., according to FlightAware tracking data. DASHCAM VIDEO CAPTURES SMALL PLANE CRASHING ON SAN JOSE HIGHWAY, INJURING THREE ON BOARD, INCLUDING CHILD Video captured from the road shows the plane’s wheels touch down on the asphalt as it speeds along Bayshore Road, its wing clipping the rear of a pickup traveling in the same direction. The truck was heading eastbound when the aircraft struck it, according to the sheriff’s office. No injuries were reported. Images shared by the sheriff’s office show the aftermath, with the small aircraft sitting on the roadway. "Thankfully, this incident had a positive outcome, and no one was injured," Lee County Sheriff Carmine Marceno said in a statement. NTSB FINDS 'NO EVIDENCE' OF MAR-A-LAGO CONNECTION AFTER FLORIDA JET CRASH KILLS NINE PEOPLE "Given the recent tragic news involving aviation accidents, we are especially grateful that everyone is safe." Marceno credited patrol deputies, FDOT Southwest Florida and Bayshore Fire Rescue for their quick response. PILOTS' PUSH TO LEVEL JET MAY HAVE TORN OFF KEY PIECE FOUND MILES FROM FLORIDA CRASH, FORMER NTSB EXPERT SAYS "We will continue working closely with our partners at the FAA as they review the circumstances surrounding this incident," he said. The Federal Aviation Administration is leading the investigation, according to the sheriff’s office. PRIVATE JET WITH 9 PEOPLE ON BOARD CRASHES JUST MILES FROM MAR-A-LAGO The close call came less than a week after a Learjet crashed Sunday, Nov. 1, in Greenacres in Palm Beach County, killing all nine people aboard.
